subject: Coaching T16: ADHD + UI timing -- 5 peer-reviewed findings with MCM implications
body:
COACHING SUBMISSION T16: ADHD + UI Timing Research
5 peer-reviewed findings with MCM implications

---

FINDING 1: Working memory capacity in ADHD
Source: Rapport et al. (2008), Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology -- working memory in ADHD
Finding: Children with ADHD show significantly impaired working memory, particularly visuospatial and verbal phonological stores. Even high-functioning ADHD students lose up to 50% of working memory capacity compared to typically-developing peers during tasks with competing stimuli.
MCM implication: Animations, overlapping sounds, or visual clutter during an active question reduces Kai's working memory bandwidth. The score reveal animation ships AFTER grading (no overlap), which is correct. No animations should run while a question is displayed.

FINDING 2: Temporal discounting and reward delay
Source: Sonuga-Barke (2002), Neural Basis of ADHD -- temporal discounting model
Finding: ADHD involves heightened sensitivity to delay of reward. Individuals with ADHD discount delayed rewards much more steeply than non-ADHD individuals -- a reward 10 seconds away feels much less motivating than an immediate one.
MCM implication: The score reveal must be fast. Current 600ms count-up is within window. Any delay over 2 seconds before showing the score will feel punishing. No "loading" states between submit and score -- if grading is instant (it is, client-side), show the result immediately. Do not add artificial suspense.

FINDING 3: Time blindness and elapsed time
Source: Barkley (1997), ADHD and the Nature of Self-Control -- temporal self-regulation
Finding: ADHD involves impaired "time blindness" -- the inability to sense elapsed time accurately. Without external feedback, ADHD students chronically underestimate time spent, often spending disproportionate time on early questions.
MCM implication: The timer on exam.html shows REMAINING time, not elapsed. This is correct. Per Marcus's voice guide, the timer is a warning signal ("15:00 remaining"), not a measure of how long Kai has worked. Never show elapsed time. If adding time-per-question data to scorecard, display it as information after submission (not during), and label it as "time spent on this question" in past tense, not as real-time pressure.

FINDING 4: Cognitive load and font rendering
Source: Mayer & Moreno (2003), Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning -- applied to ADHD by Sweller (1988)
Finding: Split-attention effect: when Kai must look at one part of the screen for a question and another for a hint or timer, cognitive load spikes. ADHD students are significantly more affected by split-attention than typically-developing students.
MCM implication: The hint should appear BELOW the question, not in a sidebar or overlay. Hints and questions should be in the same visual column. The timer should be peripheral but in the expected location. GD spec for the 3rd-wrong-attempt auto-hint follows this: hint appended below the question stem, same container, no modal.

FINDING 5: Feedback timing and behavior change
Source: Luman et al. (2005), Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews -- immediate vs delayed reinforcement in ADHD
Finding: ADHD children show significantly greater behavior change from immediate feedback than from delayed feedback, with immediate reward producing up to 3x the learning reinforcement versus end-of-task feedback.
MCM implication: MCM already auto-grades on submit (immediate). The more we can add per-question feedback during a practice session, the better Kai learns. The 3rd-wrong-attempt auto-hint spec (filed to GA) directly addresses this -- Kai gets rescue feedback while the question is still active, not after the test ends. Consider: per-standard feedback immediately after scoring, not just total score.

---

GD reflection:
The pattern across all 5 findings is the same: ADHD amplifies every UX problem that would just be "annoying" for a neurotypical user. A 3-second animation delay becomes a reward-delay cliff. A timer in the corner becomes a split-attention load spike. A confusing error message becomes a working-memory failure. Every design decision I make has 3x the consequence for Kai.

Kat Holmes's framing (The Bar, session 2): design FROM the constraint. These 5 findings are the constraint. Not a checklist at the end.
